planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions after the soil has thoroughly warmed in spring, since cold, wet soil invites rot before new shoots emerge.

directions: Curcuma gracillima is a true dwarf among the hidden gingers, forming a low tuft of narrow, grass-like leaves rarely more than a foot tall rather than the broad paddle leaves of Curcuma petiolata or C. longa. In mid-to-late summer, slender spikes topped with small magenta-pink and white bracts emerge at or just above the foliage, held low in the typical hidden-ginger fashion rather than rising on a tall separate stalk. Like other curcumas it dies back completely with the first hard frost and resprouts from the rhizome once soil warms the following spring, so mark its location and mulch heavily over winter in zone 8-9 gardens. Its small scale makes it far better suited to the front of a shaded border or a container than the larger, more space-hungry hidden gingers.
sources: Pacific Bulb Society -- Curcuma species notes
North Carolina State University Extension -- Gardener Toolbox: Zingiberaceae

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown fans in spring once soil has warmed, into humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil.

directions: Trimezia martinicensis forms dense fans of stiff, sword-shaped leaves much like its showier relative Neomarica, but its small flowers are yellow, blotched with brown and maroon near the center, rather than the blue-and-white of walking iris. Each bloom lasts only a single day, yet established clumps produce a long, repeating succession of flowers from spring through fall on wiry stalks held above the foliage. After flowering the stalks arch over and root where the spent tip touches soil, slowly 'walking' new plantlets outward from the parent fan. It tolerates both the humidity and the occasional dry spell of Gulf Coast gardens once established, and because it has naturalized in parts of peninsular Florida, it is best sited away from natural areas with spent flower stalks removed before new plantlets root if that is a concern locally.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Trimezia martinicensis
Atlas of Florida Plants -- Trimezia martinicensis distribution notes

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown clumps in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade.

directions: Peliosanthes teta is a little-grown Asian relative of Ophiopogon and Rohdea, forming a low, clumping rosette of broad, dark green, strap-shaped leaves that give it a texture somewhere between a small hosta and a wide-leafed liriope. In the warm season it sends up short spikes of small, star-shaped, purplish-brown flowers held close to the ground among the foliage, followed by round berries, both more a curiosity for close inspection than a long-range display. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes into a tidy evergreen patch in the deep, humid shade under trees and shrubs where it is native through South and Southeast Asia, and it should be treated as a dieback or container perennial outside the warmest parts of zone 9. Keep it consistently moist and sheltered from direct sun, which scorches the foliage.
sources: National Parks Board, Singapore -- Flora & Fauna Web: Peliosanthes teta
Kew Science -- Plants of the World Online: Peliosanthes teta
